lesson_title: Two Honest Answers to One Question: FIFO and Weighted Average
hook_text: Same fridge, same cans, same sales — and two different profits. Both correct.
clip_script: Zanele's tuck shop buys cooldrinks at ten rand. Then winter comes and the wholesaler's price climbs to twelve. Now there are thirty cans in her fridge — some bought at ten, some at twelve — and cold cans don't carry receipts. So what is her stock WORTH? Watch both honest answers. She bought forty cans at ten rand and twenty at twelve — six hundred and forty rand for sixty cans — and sold thirty at fifteen rand: four hundred and fifty in the till. Answer one: she always sells the oldest first, so the fridge holds the newest cans — all twenty twelve-rand cans plus ten ten-rand cans. Fridge: three hundred and forty. Profit: one hundred and fifty. Answer two: pool everything — six forty across sixty cans is about ten sixty-seven a can. Fridge: three twenty. Profit: one thirty. Two methods, twenty rand apart — and look where the twenty lives: it is exactly the gap between the two fridge values. Whatever the fridge holds, the profit line released. That is the whole secret of stock valuation: the shelf and the profit share one pot of rands. Which is why the rule is pick one method and KEEP it — because an owner who switches methods in a lean year isn't doing arithmetic anymore. She's telling stories.
visual_style: A glowing fridge with cans stacked in two coloured layers — ten-rand blue, twelve-rand orange — splitting into two side-by-side timelines; a rand note physically sliding between the fridge and the profit line to show the shared pot.
mood: Playful, crisp, quietly subversive at the close.
pacing: Quick setup, two clean calculation beats, slow reveal of the shared twenty rand, pointed ending.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and value any shelf two ways — then defend your answer.
